title: The chained woman
hook: a woman whose husband won't grant a divorce; every stream seeks solutions

segments.voice: Yesterday, the get, the written document of divorce. Your line was even the altar weeps. Did you let something sad be sad? A new week starts today, with the other side of that document. Day one thousand seventy-nine.

Rabbi Akiva is traveling, far from home, in Nehardea in Babylonia. A man there pulls him aside with a teaching he's been carrying. In the land of Israel, he's heard, only one sage lets a woman remarry on the word of a single witness that her husband has died. Go back, the man says, and tell them in my name. Akiva carries it home and repeats it before Rabban Gamaliel, and Gamaliel is glad. The Mishnah says the rule was then set: one witness is enough. Why would a court bend its own rules of evidence? Because of the woman waiting. Today: the agunah.
screen: `AKIVA IN NEHARDEA.` → `TELL THEM IN MY NAME.` → `ONE WITNESS IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Agunah. The word is usually translated the chained woman. Yesterday you heard that in Jewish law a marriage ends with a get, a document the husband gives. Here's the shadow side of that rule. If there's no get, she can't remarry under Jewish law. First, the old case: the husband who vanished. A man goes to sea, or to war, and never comes back. No body, no document. Is she a widow or a wife? The rabbis did something unusual here. Normally a court wants two witnesses. For her, they accepted one, and the Talmud gives the reason in a phrase: they were lenient because of the agunah. The law bent to free her. Second, the modern case: the husband who refuses. He's alive, the marriage is over, and he won't give the get, sometimes to punish her, sometimes to bargain. She's chained by his choice. Third, the answers, and here the streams work in their own ways. In Orthodox communities, rabbinical courts can pressure a refusing husband, and some couples now sign a prenuptial agreement that makes refusal costly. Conservative rabbis added a clause to the ketubah, and their courts have other tools. Reform Judaism generally accepts a civil divorce, so this bind doesn't arise there in the same way. And across the streams, women and rabbis have gone public, standing outside the homes and workplaces of men who refuse, asking them to give the get. Different paths, the same direction. That old story of Akiva and the single witness is why it matters. The tradition itself shows how its own rules can bend toward a woman who's waiting. Unchain her.
screen: `NO GET, NO REMARRIAGE.` · `THE VANISHED HUSBAND: ONE WITNESS.` · `THE REFUSING HUSBAND.` · `EACH STREAM, ITS OWN ANSWERS.` · then, large: `UNCHAIN HER.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: think of someone who feels trapped. Sit, and let your breath slow. Maybe it's a friend stuck in a job, a relative in a hard marriage, someone waiting on a decision another person won't make. Hold them in mind. Don't try to fix their situation. Just ask one question: what would one small key look like? A phone call. A ride. A listening hour. A name of someone who can help. Let one small, real idea come. The bell holds the time.
Agunah. The chained woman: a wife who cannot remarry because her husband has vanished or won't give a get. Today's word.
Your line: unchain her. Today, take the small key you thought of and use it: send the message, make the call, offer the ride. Day one thousand seventy-nine.
